content: In certain healthcare settings, patients may refrain from reporting issues such as pain, anxiety, or hunger because they believe no solutions are available. Early identification of palliative care needs by primary care providers is influenced by several factors, including the clinician's knowledge, skills, and communication style; the patient's communication style; the quality of the clinician-patient relationship; the patient’s perception of the clinician’s role; the level of collaboration between the primary care clinician and other healthcare professionals; and the patient’s fears and beliefs about their prognosis. Primary care providers must be skilled in identifying palliative care needs, and tools are available to assist in this process. Once these needs are identified, appropriate assessments and interventions can be implemented. However, integrating palliative care into primary healthcare (PHC) systems risks overburdening already strained primary care clinicians. To mitigate this, adequate funding is necessary to employ sufficient primary care staff and strengthen the PHC system. Evidence suggests that palliative care services, including home care, can reduce healthcare system costs, providing medical, ethical, and financial justification for integrating palliative care into PHC. Sending patients home for palliative care can place significant physical, mental, and financial strain on family caregivers. Training family members in basic nursing skills may alleviate some of this stress, but the home environment must be carefully assessed to ensure the well-being of family caregivers is not compromised. For terminally ill patients with well-controlled symptoms but families unable to provide care at home, end-of-life care at community health centers (CHCs) staffed 24/7 could be an alternative. This approach allows families to visit without the burden of providing constant care and is less expensive than hospital care. Community participation is a key component of PHC, as outlined in the Declaration of Alma-Ata. Communities possess untapped resources and energy that can be mobilized for healthcare delivery. In many countries, community health workers (CHWs) live within the same communities as patients and can provide home visits as needed. CHWs, under supervision, can be trained in a few hours to provide emotional support, monitor for uncontrolled symptoms, unmet social needs, and improper medication use, and report their observations to a supervising nurse at the CHC. Nurses can then provide instructions to patients or caregivers via mobile phone, make home visits, or consult with primary care physicians for further advice. If necessary, patients can be referred to CHCs or hospitals for higher-level palliative care. Establishing reliable communication and referral systems between all levels of the healthcare system is essential. In areas without CHWs, a network of community palliative care volunteers can be established. These volunteers, with basic training in palliative care principles, can assist primary care teams in providing and monitoring care. Some initiatives view chronic and incurable illnesses as biosocial or social problems with medical components, rather than purely medical issues. Community participation is strongest when members are empowered to take part in planning and implementing PHC in their communities. This empowerment can begin by exploring community healthcare needs and discussing community-based primary and palliative care at local meetings. Training in palliative care is essential for PHC providers. Core competencies include early identification of suffering due to serious or life-threatening illnesses, assessing palliative needs, managing common distressing symptoms (e.g., pain, dyspnea, fatigue, nausea, constipation, anxiety, confusion), knowing when to refer patients to higher levels of care, and providing culturally sensitive emotional support and future care planning for patients and families. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that all medical and nursing students receive a 30–40-hour basic palliative care course during their final year of training. Continuing education in palliative care should also be available to practicing clinicians, with incentives to complete this training. Task shifting, as recommended by WHO, involves redistributing palliative care responsibilities among PHC team members to optimize care delivery. For example, medical doctors, nurses, and CHWs can all contribute to pain management, symptom control, psychosocial support, and end-of-life care. Regular supervision is crucial to maintain high-quality care when task shifting is implemented. Examples of successful palliative care integration into PHC include programs in Thailand, Uganda, and Kerala, India. In Thailand, a strong PHC network, universal health coverage, and effective training programs have enabled nurse-led palliative home care teams to operate across the country. In Uganda, despite limited resources, NGOs have played a significant role in providing community-based palliative care, with basic services now available in 75% of districts. In Kerala, India, the Neighborhood Network in Palliative Care (NNPC) has empowered local communities to create sustainable palliative care programs, supported by government policies and training initiatives. These examples highlight the importance of community participation, adequate training, and strong healthcare infrastructure in integrating palliative care into PHC systems.
